picks.style: archaic greek chorus, aulos and krotala, agitated female voices overlapping, urgent, driving
picks.why: The panic at the walls — "Do you hear the clash of shields?" — short breathless lines built for a chorus in flight.

picks.style: martial greek chant, deep frame drums and horn, low male voices, ominous, heavy tread
picks.why: Hippomedon spinning his shield: Typhon breathing dark smoke, the rim braided with snakes, the warrior raving like a maenad.

picks.style: greek dirge, bowed lyre over a low drone, unison voices, slow, final
picks.why: "Their hatred has ceased... now truly their blood is one" — the iron from across the sea divides the brothers' estate. A closed lament.

picks.style: roman comic canticum, double pipe and plucked lyre, brash male voice, fast patter, swaggering
picks.why: The clever slave's manifesto — with rogues a rogue, with thieves a thief, wise enough to shift his very skin.

picks.style: mock-tragic patter song, tibia and hand drum, indignant declaiming voice, quick, exasperated
picks.why: "Open and throw back this gate of hell" — Bacchis and Bacchanals, sisters who suck the blood of men. A complete comic tirade.

picks.style: burlesque epic recitation, lyre and drum, boastful male voice, strutting, mock-heroic
picks.why: Chrysalus casting himself as Agamemnon and Ulysses and the old man as Troy — the play's most famous conceit, self-explaining.

picks.style: latin elegiac song, lyre and light hand percussion, wry seductive male voice, easy ambling tempo
picks.why: The proem: art guides the chariot, art instructs to love — and Cupid as a child to be schooled like Achilles under Chiron.

picks.style: roman love song, cithara and soft flute, coaxing tenor, patient, sinuous
picks.why: "Water is soft and marble hard, and yet we see soft water through hard marble eat" — persuasion by accumulation, made of proverbs.

picks.style: satirical roman air, plucked strings and tabor, sardonic voice, brisk, cutting
picks.why: "This is the golden age, all worship gold" — and Homer himself turned out of doors for arriving without a present.

picks.style: english narrative ballad, harp and fiddle, storytelling mezzo voice, steady gait, foreboding
picks.why: The Warrior's Return — Sir Walter home from the Holy Land with a strangely bloodied sword. Pure ballad, and it hooks in four stanzas.

picks.style: island lament, solo female voice over sparse frame drum and low strings, desolate, slow
picks.why: "Hail, lonely shore! hail, desert cave!... For what can misery do but die?" — a song by title and by build.

picks.style: regency parlour song, fortepiano and cello, bright soprano, buoyant, teasing
picks.why: Trochaic welcome-home stanzas that turn into a claim: fame is dear to you, but don't prefer it again to home and me.

picks.style: graveyard-school elegy, viola and chamber organ, low measured male voice, slow, grey-lit
picks.why: Sleep refusing to come, then dawn over the flowering thorn and the miners whistling out to the pit. A complete elegiac opening.

picks.style: 18th century pastoral elegy, harpsichord and strings, plaintive tenor, moderate, wistful
picks.why: Insects sipping the rainbow shower against the dart that found its entrance near the heart before the poet was twenty-two.

picks.style: roman processional hymn, lyre and double aulos, mixed choir of boys and girls, stately, bright, ceremonial
picks.why: The opening invocation of Phoebus and Diana — this is literally a hymn commissioned to be sung by a chorus.

picks.style: antiphonal hymn, two answering choirs of boys and girls, kithara and soft drum, alternating, solemn
picks.why: Boys to Apollo, girls to the Moon — the structure of the stanza is already a call and response.

picks.style: roman triumph hymn, trumpets and lyre, full choir, broad, radiant, rising
picks.why: Faith, Peace, Honour and Modesty daring to return, and Plenty appearing with her full horn — the ode's great turn.

picks.style: archaic epic recitation, single lyre, grave male voice, sparse, unhurried
picks.why: Only candidate, but it carries the Cyclopes lines: no halls of council and no laws, each man aloft in his cave making his own law.

picks.style: roman soldiers' marching chant, stamping feet and low drum, gruff male voices in unison, blunt, repetitive
picks.why: Only candidate, and it is already a chant — elephant, lion, tiger, all killed; beware the many if you do not fear the few.
